video_title: Jordi Visser: Why the S&P 500 Reign Is Officially Over
gist: Jordi Visser argues the era of public-company (S&P 500) dominance is ending as AI destroys moats and tokenization makes illiquid assets liquid, shifting money-supply growth toward private entrepreneurs and crypto holders. He frames Microsoft's offer of buyouts to ~27% of staff as a labor-versus-capital boiling point that will push governments toward taxing corporations and cutting individual taxes, expects Treasury to suppress long-end yields (bullish for Bitcoin), and flags longevity/healthcare (Eli Lilly) as his top under-followed theme.

themes.theme: End of the S&P 500 / public-company reign

insights.claim: Jordi Visser believes the S&P 500's long reign is ending, not because of the index itself but because public companies are losing out to fast-growing private companies that no longer need capital markets to raise money.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests passive US large-cap index exposure may stop compounding faster than money supply; alpha migrates to private markets.
insights.quote: we are at the end of the S&P 500's reign in my opinion. And it's not about S&P 500, it's about public companies.

insights.claim: Visser's base case is that the S&P 500 does not crash but simply stops outgrowing money supply, with incremental money-supply growth flowing to small entrepreneurs and crypto investors rather than public companies (including the Russell 2000).
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A flat-in-real-terms S&P scenario favors reallocating toward crypto and private/entrepreneurial exposure over broad equity beta.
insights.quote: let's assume the S&P 500 stops going up, which is what I think will happen, but it doesn't go down.

insights.claim: Visser says most of the S&P 500 is stagnant 'garbage', noting that homebuilders, autos ex-Tesla and retailers combined are not close to the size of a single large technology company, so the index's returns are really a tech/innovation story.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Index returns are concentrated in tech; non-tech constituents are a drag that AI disruption may worsen.
insights.quote: Most of the S&P 500 is garbage. It's companies that have not gone up for a long time.

insights.claim: Visser argues that for the first time in history the largest public companies (the Mag 7) became the biggest without taking on debt, but they now must borrow to fund the AI buildout, which he calls life support and doubts will work out, making them not the best companies to own.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Megacap tech shifting from debt-free compounders to levered capex spenders undermines their quality premium.
insights.quote: Now they've had to take debt now >> to fuel the next phase, but this is for life support for them. And I don't think it's going to work out.

insights.claim: Visser argues AI eliminates durable moats because any idea can be copied instantly, so the Mag 7's innovation moat will not be replicated and future startups will not reach Instagram-scale acquisitions.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Erosion of moats compresses terminal values and argues against paying premium multiples for incumbents' franchises.
insights.quote: A moat can't exist if it can be copied instantaneously.

insights.claim: Visser disputes that gold has outperformed the S&P 500, saying on a total-return basis with dividends the two have been roughly equal since the Great Financial Crisis, while the S&P has outperformed most other global equity markets because it holds the world's tech.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the debasement narrative that US equity gains are illusory versus hard assets.
insights.quote: Gold and S&P have been around the same since the great financial crisis.

insights.claim: Visser says comparing the S&P 500 to M2 is a poor framework because since the GFC the S&P has risen at a much higher multiple than money supply, reflecting more leverage of money flowing into capital profits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rejects a popular Bitcoin-community framing that equity gains merely track money printing.

themes.theme: Tokenization and the exploding money supply

insights.claim: Visser estimates roughly $120-150 trillion of hard currency globally against close to a quadrillion dollars of assets, and argues tokenization will make those illiquid assets liquid, causing effective money supply to expand massively over the next 10-15 years.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes money-supply growth as driven by asset liquefaction, a tailwind for tokenization platforms and crypto rails.
insights.quote: I think going forward money supply is going to explode through tokenization, not through government printing.

insights.claim: Visser envisions people eventually spending the economics of illiquid assets, such as buying a coffee with the economics of their house, citing tokenized stocks and oil exposure on Hyperliquid as early examples of the blurring line between equity and token economics.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Points to on-chain perps/tokenized-asset venues like Hyperliquid as the leading edge of the capital-structure shift.

insights.claim: Visser wants his own content business community to own part of the business via programmable money, and says he is growing less worried each day about US regulatory risk around tokenization.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Signals easing perceived regulatory risk for tokenized equity/community-ownership models.

insights.claim: Visser expects crypto investing to make ordinary people a lot of money outside Wall Street, because institutions are restricted and have not done their homework, while retail holders (he cites police officers and firemen asking about Ripple) know more about crypto than Wall Street.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies the crypto capital-formation upside accrues to early retail adopters before institutions catch up.
insights.quote: Everyone, including my son, knows more about crypto than people on Wall Street.

insights.claim: Visser says Jeff Booth's historical account of debt-based fiat makes sense but he disagrees with Booth's future view, believing abundance and democratization will come via AI-driven deflation and tokenization rather than a collapse of the system.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a bullish-abundance view from the hard-money deflationary-collapse thesis common among Bitcoiners.

insights.claim: Visser says the prevailing pattern of skeptics calling both AI and Bitcoin bubbles is consistent, and that he rarely meets anyone who believes in Bitcoin but thinks AI is a bubble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests AI and Bitcoin sentiment are correlated holder bases, relevant for cross-asset positioning.

themes.theme: Labor vs capital: Microsoft as the tell

insights.claim: According to Visser, Microsoft, with about 223,000 employees, offered roughly 60,000 (about 27%) a package to leave; at an average all-in compensation of about $400,000 that is about $24 billion a year and would return headcount to roughly 2020 levels.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A large-scale labor-to-capex swap at a megacap signals AI-driven opex cuts funding data center spend.
insights.quote: Microsoft has about 223,000 employees and they made a public announcement that they were going to give the option to 60,000

insights.claim: Visser says Microsoft's revenue tracked its headcount historically, but if it hits next year's expectations revenue will be up about 70% since 2019-2020 with flat employees, sending revenue per employee sharply higher, which he calls a direct labor-versus-capital issue.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rising revenue per employee supports margin expansion at AI adopters while pressuring labor income.

insights.claim: Visser argues Microsoft is cutting staff to pay for data centers now that AI lets tech companies need fewer employees, and that shifting income from highly taxed individuals (paying 50-60%) to lower-taxed corporations widens government deficits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI-driven labor substitution erodes the income-tax base, adding fiscal pressure and debt issuance.

insights.claim: Visser believes the labor-versus-capital and affordability crisis is reaching a boiling point globally (citing France and young people in Williamsburg, Brooklyn feeling 'trapped') and predicts next year it becomes a much bigger story.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rising political risk around affordability could drive redistributive policy shifts in 2027.
insights.quote: We're trapped in our jobs. >> We're trapped having to go to work. We're trapped not being able to afford a home.

insights.claim: Visser predicts that as corporations shed employees (e.g. a hypothetical Microsoft with 1,000 employees worth $5 trillion), lobbying power weakens and governments will tax corporations rather than individuals, effectively delivering a form of universal basic income through lower individual tax rates.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Long-run risk of materially higher corporate tax rates on AI winners, compressing after-tax margins.
insights.quote: I think corporations will end up being taxed, individuals will get tax breaks and that's the way this is all going to play out over time.

insights.claim: Visser frames AI's impact in stages: the next 5 years bring chaotic job disruption while people still need to work, though current unemployment and population-adjusted jobless claims (about 194,000, lowest on record) remain very low.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Labor data still looks strong now; AI displacement is a forward risk rather than a current macro signal.

insights.claim: Visser argues younger generations will be fine because AI agents and humanoids will act as 24/7 digital employees, reducing the burden of supporting older people via entitlements and pensions that he says has driven inflationary pressure.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames AI as structurally deflationary, countering the entitlement-driven inflation thesis.
insights.quote: We are going to have servants for us in the form of digital employees that work 24/7.

insights.claim: Visser says AI-native entrepreneurs can run many small revenue streams (e.g. 25 streams at $10,000 each) with AI agents instead of taking a $150,000 job, and that this is already happening.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Supports a long-tail solo-entrepreneur economy that benefits AI tooling and payment rails over large employers.

insights.claim: Visser says enterprise AI adoption only started this year and agentic AI only became capable around August-September, and big-bank contacts all expect AI spend-out to be a major theme next year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies the AI labor-substitution cycle is early, with most impact still ahead.

themes.theme: AI capex debt, yields and Treasury

insights.claim: Visser argues this year was the peak of concentrated hyperscaler debt needs, contrary to charts showing ever-growing issuance, because more funding will come from free cash flow, especially where compute was bought ahead and compute prices have risen; he expects hyperscaler debt needs to peak in early next year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Peaking hyperscaler issuance would ease credit-spread pressure on AI names.
insights.quote: the hypers scalers debt needs will probably peak in early next year

insights.claim: Visser notes Oracle said this week that compute economics are improving and that Oracle's CDS then had its biggest decline since the AI debt concerns began.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tightening Oracle CDS is a credit-market signal that AI-debt fears are easing.
insights.quote: And what did Oracle's CDS do? I'm going to show it this week. Had the biggest decline since this whole thing started.

insights.claim: Visser expects non-hyperscalers such as Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and pharma (citing Eli Lilly) to raise debt for their own data centers and open-source models, keeping pressure on the long end of the bond market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Broadening AI capex to enterprises sustains long-duration supply and data center demand.

insights.claim: Visser predicts Treasury Secretary Bessent will have to act in the bond market (possibly this month), shifting issuance to the front end to push long yields lower for housing, effectively yield curve control without the label, which he says is good for Bitcoin and crypto.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Stealth yield curve control and front-end issuance would be a liquidity tailwind for Bitcoin and duration assets.
insights.quote: we're just going to get this, whatever you want to call it, yield curve control, but without it being this.

insights.claim: Visser says his earlier call that the AI 'fireworks show is over' was right in that there is no more easy money in the AI trade, as funds that chased AI in Q1 got caught in the deleveraging from June, which he views as a big positive for Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests marginal speculative capital may rotate from crowded AI trades toward Bitcoin.
insights.quote: there's no more easy money in the AI trade.

insights.claim: Visser dismisses the 'stealth bear market' in memory stocks as a normal pullback, noting names like Micron are still up 7-10x from a year ago after being up about 20x at the peak.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames memory-stock weakness as consolidation rather than an AI bubble bursting.

insights.claim: Visser says private credit and commercial real estate fears faded because debt can be worked out over long periods rather than hitting the market at once, which he calls the biggest change in markets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues credit doom scenarios are overstated because extend-and-pretend defuses forced selling.

insights.claim: Visser says he has cut his macro podcast listening by about 95% because nearly all macro analysis assumes innovation will not accelerate, which he believes is wrong.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Warns that consensus macro models may systematically underprice AI-driven productivity and deflation.
insights.quote: If someone doesn't use AI every day and they don't have a a clearcut conversation piece about AI, I can't listen to them

insights.claim: Visser predicts Eli Lilly will become the biggest company in the world within 5 years, driven by its AI investments and the intersection of AI with healthcare.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explicit single-stock conviction call on Eli Lilly as an AI-plus-longevity winner.
insights.quote: I think Eli Liy will be the biggest company in the world over the next in the next 5 years

insights.claim: Visser expects longevity to become a major story next year and asks what happens to Medicare, Medicaid and the health system if all disease is being cured a decade from now, a question he says almost no macro analysts address.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Second-order implications for entitlement spending, insurers and healthcare business models are underexplored.

insights.claim: Visser notes the healthcare sector has started to outperform and that it outperformed significantly when the dot-com bubble unwound and during the GFC, making it an easier place to be.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Healthcare as a defensive rotation if tech/AI leadership falters.
insights.quote: The health care sector has started to outperform.

insights.claim: Visser says the Bitcoin community lacks a credible leader or spokesperson on the quantum computing risk, leaving the narrative open to misinformation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An unaddressed quantum narrative is a sentiment overhang on Bitcoin.
insights.quote: it's very frustrating that the community that someone hasn't been a leader in this and kind of taken the front hasn't taken the wheel

insights.claim: Visser criticizes skeptics who give Bitcoin no chance to outperform while assuming the S&P 500 will make money forever, and endorses Michael Saylor's view that a capital-structure change is under way.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reinforces the thesis of relative rotation from public equities to Bitcoin/tokenized capital.

insights.claim: Visser frames high-profile 'Bitcoin to zero' calls (e.g. from Chamath and the All-In hosts) and doomer narratives as attention-driven engagement farming, noting doomers are often those rooting for declines.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests treating celebrity bearish Bitcoin calls as sentiment noise rather than signal.
